building.label: Building
building.description: A fixed electricity demand (lights, plugs, appliances).

fields.name: load_profile
fields.label: Load profile
fields.help: Hour-by-hour demand recorded in a real building.
fields.source: CityLearn 2022 dataset, Building_1.csv

fields.name: scale
fields.label: Scale factor
fields.help: Multiplies the profile. Homes: number of similar homes. Commercial profiles given per 1,000 m²: floor area in m² divided by 1,000 (e.g. 2.5 for 2,500 m²).

data_center.label: Data center
data_center.description:
A data center: servers (IT load) plus cooling and other overhead, set by the PUE.

    Facility power = IT power x PUE. The PUE is held constant, so cooling follows the IT load
    but not the weather (real cooling rises on hot afternoons). The UPS battery and backup
    generator are separate components: add a battery with a minimum charge as the backup reserve.

fields.name: it_load_profile
fields.label: IT load profile
fields.help: Measured server power. The ESIF profiles are a ~3 MW supercomputer centre in Colorado.
fields.source: NLR (NREL) HPC Facility PUE Data, it_power_kw, https://data.openei.org/submissions/8616

fields.name: it_scale
fields.label: IT scale factor
fields.help: Multiplies the IT profile. 2 means twice the servers of the measured site.

fields.name: pue
fields.label: PUE (total power / IT power)
fields.help: 1.54 is the 2025 industry average; best liquid-cooled sites reach about 1.05-1.1. Everything above 1 is cooling, fans, pumps, lights and losses.
fields.source: Uptime Institute Global Data Center Survey 2025 (UII Keynote Report 180), p. 7, Fig. 2: weighted average annual PUE 1.54, n=681

heat_pump.label: Heat pump
heat_pump.description:
An electric heat pump for space heating and hot water, with a heat buffer (tank).

    Heat demand = a When2Heat profile x the annual heat demand. Electricity = heat / COP, using the COP of the
    chosen heat pump type in that hour. The tank lets the controller heat earlier than needed (when power is
    cheap or solar is spare) and use the stored heat later. If the heat pump cannot cover the demand (too
    small, or limited by the grid operator), the shortfall is recorded as unmet heat.

fields.name: heat_profile
fields.label: Heat demand profile
fields.help: Hourly shape of space heating plus hot water for a building type and country.
fields.source: When2Heat (Ruhnau, Hirth, Praktiknjo 2019, Scientific Data 6:189), Open Power System Data 2023-07-27, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0199-y

fields.name: annual_heat_kwh
fields.label: Annual heat demand
fields.help: Heat needed in a year for space heating and hot water. 15,730 kWh is the average gas use of a 130 m² single-family house in Germany; gas use includes boiler losses, so the heat actually needed is somewhat lower.
fields.source: co2online Heizspiegel 2025 (with Deutscher Mieterbund and BMWK), as reported by t-online, 23.09.2025: 130 m² single-family house, about 15,730 kWh of gas per year

fields.name: cop_profile
fields.label: Heat pump type (COP)
fields.help: Coefficient of performance per hour: kWh of heat per kWh of electricity. Depends on the heat source (air or ground), the outdoor temperature and the heating circuit (radiators need hotter water than floor heating, so the COP is lower).
fields.source: When2Heat (Ruhnau, Hirth, Praktiknjo 2019, Scientific Data 6:189), Open Power System Data 2023-07-27, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-019-0199-y

fields.name: max_power_kw
fields.label: Max electric power
fields.help: Electric power of the heat pump. Empty = sized to cover the coldest hour of the simulated period exactly (no spare capacity for pre-heating then).

fields.name: buffer_kwh
fields.label: Heat buffer (tank) size
fields.help: Heat the tank can store and release later. About 7 kWh is a 300-litre water tank used over 20 °C.
fields.source: Example choice; water stores about 4.19 kJ per kg per kelvin, so 300 kg x 20 K x 4.19 kJ/(kg·K) = 7.0 kWh

fields.name: buffer_initial
fields.label: Initial tank charge
fields.help: Share of the buffer that is full at the start.
fields.source: Example choice

fields.name: capacity_kwp
fields.label: Installed capacity
fields.help: Peak DC power of the panels.
fields.source: CityLearn citylearn_challenge_2022_phase_1 schema.json, Building_1 pv.nominal_power

fields.name: profile
fields.label: Solar profile
fields.help: Generation per kWp, hour by hour, from the same dataset as the loads.
fields.source: CityLearn 2022 dataset, Building_1.csv solar_generation

fields.name: capacity_kwh
fields.label: Usable capacity
fields.source: CityLearn citylearn_challenge_2022_phase_1 schema.json, Building_1 electrical_storage.capacity

fields.name: power_kw
fields.label: Max charge/discharge power
fields.source: CityLearn citylearn_challenge_2022_phase_1 schema.json, Building_1 electrical_storage.nominal_power

fields.name: round_trip_efficiency
fields.label: Round-trip efficiency
fields.help: Share of energy put in that comes back out. Losses split equally between charging and discharging.
fields.source: CityLearn citylearn_challenge_2022_phase_1 schema.json, Building_1 electrical_storage.efficiency (CityLearn takes the square root as one-way efficiency)

fields.name: soc_min
fields.label: Minimum state of charge
fields.help: Never discharge below this fraction of capacity.

fields.name: soc_max
fields.label: Maximum state of charge
fields.help: Never charge above this fraction of capacity.

fields.name: soc_initial
fields.label: Initial state of charge
fields.source: CityLearn default initial_soc = 0

fields.name: chemistry
fields.label: Cell chemistry (for wear)
fields.help: Which ageing model prices battery wear. lfp: lithium iron phosphate, most new stationary storage. nmc: nickel manganese cobalt, more common in older and car batteries; ages faster in the models used.
fields.source: NREL BLAST-Lite models Lfp_Gr_250AhPrismatic and NMC_Gr_75Ah_A, fitted to Gasper et al. 2023, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.est.2023.109042

fields.name: replacement_cost_per_kwh
fields.label: Replacement cost
fields.help: What the battery system costs per usable kWh, in the site's currency. Wear = this value used up as the battery ages. Empty = by size, EUR sites only: 1,200 (home, up to 30 kWh), 580-710 (commercial), 380-464 (large-scale); 2022 prices excluding VAT, higher than today's.
fields.source: Figgener et al. 2023, The development of battery storage systems in Germany: a market review (status 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.06762: 2022 mean prices per usable kWh, excl. VAT

fields.name: end_of_life_capacity
fields.label: End of life at
fields.help: Share of the original capacity at which the battery counts as worn out. Warranties use 60-80%.
fields.source: LG Energy Solution RESU12 warranty: 80% energy retention after 10 years or 30 MWh throughput

fields.name: temperature_c
fields.label: Battery temperature
fields.help: Assumed constant. Warmer batteries age faster. The ageing models were fitted between 10 and 45 °C.
fields.source: Example choice (indoor installation); fitting range from the BLAST-Lite model notes

ev_charger.label: EV charger
ev_charger.description: One EV charging point with the cars that visit it.

fields.name: max_power_kw
fields.label: Max charging power
fields.source: CityLearn citylearn_challenge_2022_phase_all_plus_evs schema.json, charger_1_1 max_charging_power

fields.name: efficiency
fields.label: Charging efficiency
fields.help: Share of grid energy that reaches the car battery.
fields.source: CityLearn citylearn_challenge_2022_phase_all_plus_evs schema.json, charger_1_1 efficiency

fields.name: sessions
fields.label: EV sessions
fields.help: Which cars arrive, when they leave, and how much energy they need.
fields.source: CityLearn 2022 EV dataset, charger_1_1.csv

fields.name: phases
fields.label: Phases
fields.help: Three-phase chargers spread their load over L1-L3; single-phase chargers put it all on one phase.

fields.name: phase
fields.label: Phase for single-phase charging
fields.help: Used by single-phase chargers, and by single-phase cars on a three-phase charger (they draw from one phase only). Spread chargers over L1-L3 to balance the load.

fields.name: min_current_a
fields.label: Minimum charging current
fields.help: Chargers cannot charge below this current per phase; they pause instead.
fields.source: IEC 61851-1: the lowest current a charger may signal to the car is 6 A

fields.name: bidirectional
fields.label: Bidirectional (V2H / V2G)
fields.help: Lets a plugged-in car give energy back to the site (vehicle-to-home) at up to the charger's power, but only while it can still be charged to its target by departure. Needs a bidirectional charger and car. Assumed to be a DC charger, which can discharge at any power up to its rating (the 6 A minimum applies to AC charging only).

fields.name: v2g_max_kwh_per_visit
fields.label: Max energy borrowed per visit
fields.help: Only for bidirectional chargers. Upper limit on energy taken from one car during one visit, to protect the driver's range and the car battery.
fields.source: Example choice

grid.name: import_limit_kw
grid.label: Import limit
grid.help: Maximum power the site may draw (connection or transformer rating). Empty = unlimited.

grid.name: export_limit_kw
grid.label: Export limit
grid.help: Maximum power the site may feed back. Solar is curtailed above it. Empty = unlimited.

grid.name: fuse_a
grid.label: Fuse per phase
grid.help: Main fuse rating per phase (three-phase, 230 V to neutral). EV charging is slowed so no phase exceeds it. Empty = not checked.

grid.name: dimming
grid.label: Grid-operator dimming (§14a, Germany)
grid.help: Simulates the grid operator limiting controllable devices during a daily window: EV chargers, heat pumps and batteries (while charging) rated above 4.2 kW. direct: each device is limited to 4.2 kW (heat pumps above 11 kW to 40% of their power). ems: the devices together are limited to 4.2 kW + (n - 1) x simultaneity factor x 4.2 kW, and the energy management system shares it out.
grid.source: BNetzA decision BK6-22-300 of 27.11.2023, Anlage 1, sections 2.4.1 (devices above 4.2 kW) and 4.5 (minimum power 4.2 kW; 0.4 x power above 11 kW; EMS formula with simultaneity factors 0.8 for 2 devices down to 0.45 for 9 or more)

grid.name: dimming_start_hour
grid.label: Dimming window start
grid.help: Real dimming is rare and comes at short notice; a daily window is a stress test, not a forecast.

tariff.name: price_adder
tariff.label: Price adder
tariff.help: Added to every import price: grid fees, taxes, supplier margin. Spot-price profiles need this to look like a real dynamic tariff. Enter your tariff's value.

tariff.name: export_price
tariff.label: Export price
tariff.help: What exported energy earns (e.g. a feed-in tariff). German examples use the EEG rate for new small rooftop systems.

tariff.name: export_unpaid_at_negative_prices
tariff.label: No export pay at negative spot prices
tariff.help: German rule for new systems (since Feb 2025) once a smart meter is fitted: exported energy earns nothing while the day-ahead spot price is negative.
tariff.source: § 51 (1) EEG 2023 (Solarspitzengesetz, BGBl. 2025 I Nr. 51): 'Fuer Zeitraeume, in denen der Spotmarktpreis negativ ist, verringert sich der anzulegende Wert auf null'; § 51 (2) Nr. 1: systems below 100 kW only from the year after a smart meter is fitted. https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/eeg_2014/__51.html

tariff.name: demand_charge_per_kw_month
tariff.label: Demand charge
tariff.help: Charged on each month's highest import (per time step). Common for commercial sites. Enter your tariff's value; there is no default.

tariff.name: network_fee_profile
tariff.label: Time-variable network fee (§14a Modul 3)
tariff.help: Optional. Adds a time-of-day network fee (low / standard / high tier) to every imported kWh, from a real German grid operator's 2026 price sheet. If you use it, leave the network fee out of the price adder. Empty = none.

tariff.name: demand_charge_profile
tariff.label: Peak-window demand charge (profile id)
tariff.help: Optional, on top of the demand charge above. A 'demand' profile giving a rate per kW per month for each hour (0 outside the window), e.g. urdb/xcel_co_pg_demand. Each month, each rate is charged on the highest import during the hours that carry it. Empty = none.

controller.name: battery
controller.label: Battery strategy
controller.help: idle: never used. self_consumption: store spare solar, use it when short. price_arbitrage: also charge from the grid at the day's cheapest hours and discharge at the most expensive. peak_shaving: keep grid import under a threshold. mpc: model predictive control, plans the battery and all EV charging together over the next hours with a linear program and re-plans regularly (the EV strategy below is then ignored).

controller.name: peak_threshold_kw
controller.label: Peak-shaving threshold
controller.help: Only used by peak_shaving. Target ceiling for grid import.

controller.name: mpc_horizon_hours
controller.label: MPC planning horizon
controller.help: Only used by mpc. How far ahead it plans. EMHASS recommends a horizon of at least five optimisation steps; 24 h covers a daily price and solar cycle.
controller.source: Example choice; EMHASS documentation: prediction horizon at least 5 x the optimisation time step

controller.name: mpc_replan_minutes
controller.label: MPC re-plan interval
controller.help: Only used by mpc. How often it re-optimises (also immediately when a car arrives). Shorter is more responsive but slower to simulate.

controller.name: mpc_execution
controller.label: MPC execution
controller.help: Only used by mpc. plan: follow the optimiser's battery plan; the battery takes up forecast errors. hybrid: behave like the self-consumption rule (store all spare solar, cover the home from the battery) and let the optimiser only add to it: charge more (e.g. from the grid before an expensive stretch) or hold energy back as a reserve. Never stores less solar than the rule would. cautious: plan for a forecast that may be wrong: use the meter for the current step; never let the battery trade extra with the grid to make up for a forecast error; value energy left at the end of the plan net of the wear of using it; store energy now rather than later when the cost is the same (the last two change the plan itself, not only how it is followed).
controller.source: hybrid: design choice, local self-consumption control with a planning layer on top, as in the layered architectures on the Learn page 'Control layers and time scales'. cautious: our own design, tuned on drivers the full-year study does not use (results/study_home_de/README_cautious.md)

controller.name: mpc_scenarios
controller.label: MPC scenarios
controller.help: Only used by mpc with realistic forecasts. 1: plan for one forecast. More: plan for several possible futures at once, each replayed from one of the last days (that day's load, that day's solar forecast error, that day's car visits), committing only to the next re-plan interval and minimising the average cost. Slower roughly in proportion.
controller.source: Two-stage scenario-based stochastic MPC (scenario approach: Campi et al. 2009); the number is an example choice

controller.name: mpc_wear_cost
controller.label: MPC prices battery wear
controller.help: Only used by mpc. Charge each kWh cycled through the battery at its wear price (replacement cost x capacity lost per cycle, from the battery's ageing model), so the plan only cycles when it pays.

controller.name: forecast
controller.label: Forecasts
controller.help: What controllers know about the future. perfect: the true future (an upper bound). realistic: only what a real system would know: load = the most recent day repeated; solar = the weather forecast from about a day earlier; day-ahead prices only once published (about 13:00 for the next day); cars only once plugged in. Affects the rules that look ahead (cheapest hours, arbitrage) and mpc.

controller.name: heat_pump
controller.label: Heat pump strategy
controller.help: on_demand: heat when needed, the tank is not used. cheap_hours: fill the tank in the cheapest quarter of the next 24 h and draw on it in the dearest quarter. solar_surplus: fill the tank with spare solar. With mpc, heat pumps run on demand (the planner does not schedule them yet).

controller.name: ev_discharge
controller.label: Car discharging (bidirectional chargers)
controller.help: Only for chargers marked bidirectional. high_prices: a plugged-in car covers the site's grid import when the price is in the dearer half of the next 24 h, as long as it can still reach its target by departure. never: cars only charge. The mpc controller does not discharge cars yet.

controller.name: ev
controller.label: EV charging strategy
controller.help: as_fast_as_possible: full power on arrival. spread_until_departure: the lowest steady power that still finishes by departure. cheapest_hours: charge in the cheapest time steps before departure. solar_surplus: charge from spare solar, and at full power only when needed to finish by departure.
